Scope extension: under the AI-12 area scope note, this requirement applies beyond neural networks. AI-12.2 additionally applies to AI systems implemented with other statistical machine learning models, including gradient-boosted trees, random forests, and support vector machines, because these model families exhibit the same confidence miscalibration failure mode. A system built on gradient boosting or a random forest is subject to confidence calibration even where no neural network component is present.
[V.AI-12.2] CONFIDENCE CALIBRATION
The AI system shall verify confidence calibration by analysis and test.
The analysis shall confirm calibration error is measured against actual prediction
accuracy, calibration thresholds are established per Section 5.1 (Threshold
Selection Guidance), and any calibration techniques applied (such as temperature
scaling, Platt scaling, or isotonic regression) are justified.
The test shall demonstrate that model confidence outputs are calibrated against
actual accuracy on representative held-out data and that calibration error remains
within the established thresholds.
Success Criteria: The verification shall be considered successful when the analysis
and test show that confidence calibration is validated against actual accuracy on
representative held-out data, calibration error is documented, and any calibration
techniques applied are justified.

entries.title: Neural Network Explainability Methods
entries.text:
[R.AI-12.3] NEURAL NETWORK EXPLAINABILITY METHODS
The AI system shall implement explainability methods appropriate to the neural
network architecture and decision criticality, with method selection documented
and justified. For Safety-Critical AI functions, the AI system shall document the
rationale for selecting neural network architectures over inherently interpretable
alternatives (decision trees, rule-based systems, linear models) when interpretable
alternatives could achieve required performance.
Rationale: Neural networks present inherent explainability challenges because
decision logic is distributed across learned weights rather than explicit rules. Post-hoc methods such as SHAP, LIME, attention visualization, and layer-wise relevance
propagation provide explanations of individual predictions but do not constitute
proof of correct decision logic. For high-criticality functions, the choice to use a
neural network rather than an interpretable alternative is itself a design decision
requiring justification.
[V.AI-12.3] NEURAL NETWORK EXPLAINABILITY METHODS
The AI system shall verify neural network explainability methods by inspection and
test.
The inspection shall confirm explainability methods appropriate to the architecture
and decision criticality are documented with selection rationale, and that any
Safety-Critical use of a neural network over an inherently interpretable alternative
is justified per AI-8 (Explainability).
The test shall demonstrate that the implemented explainability methods generate
explanations for individual predictions as documented.
Success Criteria: The verification shall be considered successful when the
inspection and test show that explainability methods are implemented and
validated, method selection rationale is documented, and any Safety-Critical use of
neural networks over interpretable alternatives is justified per AI-8 (Explainability).

entries.title: Training Integrity
entries.text:
[R.AI-12.4] TRAINING INTEGRITY
The AI system shall implement and document training integrity controls including:
documented overfitting indicators and the threshold beyond which retraining is
required; documented relationship between model architecture complexity and
training data volume; documented random seeds and training configurations to
enable reproducibility; and validation set contamination controls beyond [R.AI-1.1]
(Dataset Separation) and [R.AI-1.2] (Partition Use Restriction), specifically
addressing hyperparameter tuning on validation data and architecture decisions
informed by validation performance.
Rationale: Neural network and other statistical machine learning training
introduces risks not present in traditional software development. Models with
sufficient capacity can memorize training data rather than learning generalizable
patterns. Hyperparameter tuning effectively incorporates validation information
into the model. Stochastic training processes introduce reproducibility concerns.
These risks require specific controls beyond the algorithm-agnostic dataset
partitioning requirements.
Scope extension: under the AI-12 area scope note, this requirement applies beyond neural networks. AI-12.4 additionally applies to AI systems implemented with other statistical machine learning models, including gradient-boosted trees, random forests, and support vector machines, because these model families exhibit the same overfitting and memorization failure modes. A system built on gradient boosting or a random forest is subject to training integrity controls even where no neural network component is present.
[V.AI-12.4] TRAINING INTEGRITY
The AI system shall verify training integrity by inspection and analysis.
The inspection shall confirm training integrity controls are documented, including
overfitting indicators and the retraining threshold, the relationship between
architecture complexity and training data volume, random seeds and training
configurations enabling reproducibility, and validation set contamination controls
beyond AI-1.1 (Dataset Separation) and AI-1.2 (Partition Use Restriction).
The analysis shall confirm the documented controls were applied during
development and are verifiable from training records.
Success Criteria: The verification shall be considered successful when the
inspection and analysis show that training integrity controls are documented,
applied during development, and verifiable from training records.

entries.title: Neural Network Out-Of-Distribution Detection Extensions
entries.text:
[R.AI-12.5] NEURAL NETWORK OUT-OF-DISTRIBUTION DETECTION EXTENSIONS
The AI system shall implement out-of-distribution detection methods appropriate
to neural network architectures, recognizing that softmax confidence alone is
insufficient for OOD detection. OOD detection for neural networks shall use
methods that account for the tendency of neural networks to produce high-confidence predictions on inputs far from the training distribution, such as
ensemble disagreement, energy-based methods, feature-space distance metrics,
or deep generative model likelihood.
Rationale: Neural networks often produce high softmax confidence scores on
inputs outside the training distribution. Standard OOD detection per [R.AI-6.2]
requires neural-network-specific extensions to be effective.
[V.AI-12.5] NEURAL NETWORK OUT-OF-DISTRIBUTION DETECTION EXTENSIONS
The AI system shall verify neural network out-of-distribution detection extensions
by test.
The test shall demonstrate that the out-of-distribution detection methods are
effective on representative out-of-distribution test data, account for the tendency
of neural networks to produce high-confidence predictions on inputs far from the
training distribution, and that the chosen method (such as ensemble disagreement,
energy-based methods, feature-space distance metrics, or deep generative model
likelihood) is justified relative to the neural network architecture and extends the
standard detection required by AI-6.2.
Success Criteria: The verification shall be considered successful when the test
shows that out-of-distribution detection methods are validated on representative
out-of-distribution test data and the chosen method is justified relative to the
neural network architecture.

entries.title: Adversarial Vulnerability Mitigation
entries.text:
[R.AI-12.6] ADVERSARIAL VULNERABILITY MITIGATION
The AI system shall implement adversarial robustness measures specific to neural
network attack classes, including testing against gradient-based attacks (FGSM,
PGD, C&W) and gradient-free attacks. Adversarial defenses shall be evaluated for
gradient masking, where defenses appear to reduce gradient-based attack success
but do not actually improve robustness.
Rationale: Neural networks are uniquely susceptible to adversarial examples:
inputs with imperceptible perturbations that cause dramatic misclassification. This
vulnerability is fundamental to gradient-based learning and cannot be fully
eliminated. Some adversarial defenses create a false sense of security by masking
gradients rather than improving robustness, requiring evaluation with gradient-free
attacks. Neural-network-specific adversarial measures supplement [R.AI-7.2]
(Adversarial Input Manipulation Protection).
[V.AI-12.6] ADVERSARIAL VULNERABILITY MITIGATION
The AI system shall verify adversarial vulnerability mitigation by test.
The test shall demonstrate that adversarial robustness is evaluated against both
gradient-based attack classes (such as FGSM, PGD, and C&W) and gradient-free
attack classes, that apparent robustness is not attributable to gradient masking,
and that residual vulnerability is documented, supplementing the protection
required by AI-7.2 (Adversarial Input Manipulation Protection).
Success Criteria: The verification shall be considered successful when the test
shows that adversarial robustness is validated against both gradient-based and
gradient-free attack classes, gradient masking is excluded as the source of any
apparent robustness, and residual vulnerability is documented.

entries.title: Generative Model Hallucination Constraints
entries.text:
[R.AI-12.7] GENERATIVE MODEL HALLUCINATION CONSTRAINTS
For neural networks that generate outputs (text, trajectories, plans, code, images),
the AI system shall implement domain-specific hallucination constraints including
physical plausibility checks (conservation laws, kinematic limits, domain-specific
bounds), cross-validation with independent sensors or models where available,
confidence-bounded outputs (refusing to generate beyond confidence thresholds),
and output format constraints that limit the space of generable outputs to
verifiable forms.
Rationale: Generative neural models can produce plausible-seeming outputs that
are factually incorrect or physically infeasible. Hallucination detection per [R.AI-5]
requires generative-model-specific constraints to be effective in safety-critical
contexts.
[V.AI-12.7] GENERATIVE MODEL HALLUCINATION CONSTRAINTS
The AI system shall verify generative model hallucination constraints by analysis
and test.
The analysis shall confirm the documented constraints include physical plausibility
checks (conservation laws, kinematic limits, domain-specific bounds), cross-validation with independent sensors or models where available, confidence-bounded outputs, and output format constraints that limit generable outputs to
verifiable forms, supplementing the hallucination detection required by AI-5.
The test shall demonstrate that the implemented constraints bound the system’s
output space within verifiable limits per the operational context.
Success Criteria: The verification shall be considered successful when the analysis
and test show that generative output constraints are documented, implemented,
and demonstrated to bound the system’s output space within verifiable limits per
the operational context.

entries.title: Deployment Transformation Validation (Neural Network Considerations)
entries.text:
[R.AI-12.8] DEPLOYMENT TRANSFORMATION VALIDATION (NEURAL NETWORK
CONSIDERATIONS)
Neural network deployment transformations shall be validated per [R.AI-4.7]
(Deployment Format Validation), with neural-network-specific attention to:
quantization sensitivity (per-layer impact analysis, post-quantization calibration on
representative data); pruning effects (validation that pruned models do not exhibit
different failure modes than original models); knowledge distillation (validation that
distilled student models preserve teacher model behavior on out-of-distribution
inputs and edge cases); and framework conversion (numerical equivalence
validation between source and target frameworks with documented acceptable
tolerances).
Rationale: Neural networks are particularly sensitive to deployment-format
transformations. Reducing precision can cause catastrophic accuracy degradation
in some layers, pruning can introduce different failure modes, distillation may not
preserve out-of-distribution behavior, and framework conversion can introduce
numerical differences due to operator implementation variations. AI-4.7
establishes the general normative requirement; this sub-requirement specifies the
neural-network-specific concerns.
[V.AI-12.8] DEPLOYMENT TRANSFORMATION VALIDATION (NEURAL NETWORK
CONSIDERATIONS)
The AI system shall verify deployment transformation validation by test, per [V.AI-4.7] (Deployment Format Validation).
The test shall demonstrate the validation evidence required by [V.AI-4.7], with
neural-network-specific attention to quantization sensitivity (per-layer impact
analysis and post-quantization calibration on representative data), pruning effects
(confirmation that pruned models do not exhibit different failure modes than the
original), knowledge distillation (confirmation that distilled student models preserve
teacher behavior on out-of-distribution inputs and edge cases), and framework
conversion (numerical equivalence between source and target frameworks within
documented tolerances).
Success Criteria: The verification shall be considered successful when the test
shows that deployment transformations satisfy [V.AI-4.7] with neural-networkspecific validation evidence demonstrating that the quantization, pruning,
distillation, and framework-conversion concerns are addressed.

entries.title: AI-13: Continuous Learning and Adaptation (area overview and source standards)
entries.text:
3.3 AI-13: CONTINUOUS LEARNING AND ADAPTATION REQUIREMENTS
[R.AI-13] CONTINUOUS LEARNING AND ADAPTATION REQUIREMENTS
The AI system will, when implementing continuous learning or adaptation during
operations, control the conditions under which learning occurs, validate what is
being learned, preserve the ability to detect and recover from learning that
produces degraded behavior, and maintain transparency over the system’s learning
history.
Continuously-learning systems update their model parameters during operation
based on observed data. ISO/IEC 22989:2022 5.11.9.2 defines continuous learning as
incremental training that occurs during operation. While continuous learning
enables AI systems to adapt to operational environments and address drift
(improving mission effectiveness when properly controlled), it introduces failure
modes that statically-trained systems do not exhibit, including catastrophic
forgetting, learning data drift, online learning instability, and the inability to verify
the operational model against a fixed validation baseline. The following sub-requirements apply to AI systems implementing continuous learning during
operations.
Related Domain Standards
•
General: ISO/IEC 22989:2022 5.11.9.2; ISO/IEC 5338:2023
•
Aerospace: NPR 7150.2D §4 (Software Lifecycle Processes); NASA-STD8739.8B (Software Assurance); current NASA guidance heavily restricts post-deployment learning; framework-defined for continuous learning
•
Aviation: FAA AI Safety Roadmap, p.10 (“Differentiate Between Learned AI and
Learning AI” principle); directly addresses learning-AI safety assurance
methodology
•
Automotive: ISO 21448:2022 §13 (Operation phase activities) for field-monitoring of evolving systems; UNECE WP.29 R157 §5.2 for post-market
ALKS changes
•
Medical: FDA AI-Enabled Device Software Functions guidance Section III
(TPLC Approach: General Principles); FDA Predetermined Change Control
Plan (PCCP) Guidance; central FDA framework for post-market AI/ML
changes
•
Industrial: ISO 13849-1 (Functional safety of control systems); does not
address continuous learning; framework-defined

entries.title: Continuous Learning Permission Criteria
entries.text:
[R.AI-13.1] CONTINUOUS LEARNING PERMISSION CRITERIA
The AI system shall declare the conditions under which continuous learning is
permitted, including the system classification tier, the operational scenarios in
which learning may occur, the data sources from which learning may proceed, and
the controls required at each tier. Safety-Critical AI continuous learning requires
rollback capability, approval for model updates prior to activation, shadow mode
validation before operational use, and automated performance bounds monitoring.
Mission-Critical AI continuous learning requires performance monitoring per AI-4,
automated rollback at defined thresholds, logging of all model updates, and
periodic review of learning trajectory. Operational Support AI continuous learning
requires baseline performance tracking and anomaly alerting for significant
behavior changes.
Rationale: Continuous learning has different risk profiles depending on system
classification and operational context. Permission criteria scale the required
controls to the consequences of degraded learning outcomes.
[V.AI-13.1] CONTINUOUS LEARNING PERMISSION CRITERIA
The AI system shall verify continuous learning permission criteria by inspection.
The inspection shall confirm the permission criteria declare the system
classification tier, the operational scenarios in which learning may occur, the
permitted data sources, and the controls required at each tier, and that the
controls are classification-appropriate (Safety-Critical AI requiring rollback
capability, pre-activation approval, shadow mode validation, and automated
performance bounds monitoring; Mission-Critical AI requiring performance
monitoring per AI-4, automated rollback at defined thresholds, update logging, and
periodic learning-trajectory review; and Operational Support AI requiring baseline
performance tracking and anomaly alerting).
Success Criteria: The verification shall be considered successful when the
inspection shows that continuous learning permission criteria are documented,
classification-appropriate, and enforced by system controls.

entries.title: Runtime Learning Controls
entries.text:
[R.AI-13.2] RUNTIME LEARNING CONTROLS
The AI system shall implement runtime controls that prevent learning when defined
preconditions are not met, including controls for safety-critical operational
windows, controls when learning data sources are suspect, and controls when
system confidence is below validated thresholds.
Rationale: Continuous learning permitted under all conditions risks incorporating
poisoned data, learning during anomalous operational states, or amplifying low-confidence behavior. Runtime controls operationalize the permission criteria
declared under AI-13.1.
[V.AI-13.2] RUNTIME LEARNING CONTROLS
The AI system shall verify runtime learning controls by test.
The test shall demonstrate that runtime controls prevent learning when defined
preconditions are not met, including during safety-critical operational windows,
when learning data sources are suspect, and when system confidence is below
validated thresholds, operationalizing the permission criteria declared under AI-13.1.
Success Criteria: The verification shall be considered successful when the test
shows that runtime learning controls prevent learning under each documented
precondition violation through test scenarios.

entries.title: Learning Data Validation
entries.text:
[R.AI-13.3] LEARNING DATA VALIDATION
The AI system shall validate learning data quality before incorporating it into model
updates, including data freshness (recency relative to operational distribution),
source legitimacy (trusted data origin), and absence of poisoning indicators
(anomaly detection on learning data prior to use).
Rationale: Learning data quality directly determines what the model learns.
Without validation, continuous learning is vulnerable to data poisoning, distribution
shift in learning data, and incorporation of stale data that misrepresents current
operational conditions.
[V.AI-13.3] LEARNING DATA VALIDATION
The AI system shall verify learning data validation by test and analysis.
The analysis shall confirm the validation criteria address data freshness (recency
relative to the operational distribution), source legitimacy (trusted data origin), and
poisoning indicators (anomaly detection on learning data prior to use).
The test shall demonstrate that learning data failing the freshness, legitimacy, or
poisoning checks is rejected before incorporation into model updates.
Success Criteria: The verification shall be considered successful when the test and
analysis show that learning data validation is implemented and demonstrated to
reject learning data that fails freshness, legitimacy, or poisoning checks.

entries.title: Catastrophic Forgetting Mitigation
entries.text:
[R.AI-13.4] CATASTROPHIC FORGETTING MITIGATION
The AI system shall implement and verify mitigations against catastrophic
forgetting (loss of previously-validated capabilities through new learning), using
methods such as elastic weight consolidation, progressive neural networks, replay
buffers, or other techniques appropriate to the model architecture and learning
paradigm.
Rationale: Per ISO/IEC 22989:2022, continuous learning systems are susceptible
to catastrophic forgetting where new learning overwrites previously acquired
knowledge. Without mitigation, continuous learning can degrade validated
capabilities even as it improves performance on new tasks.
[V.AI-13.4] CATASTROPHIC FORGETTING MITIGATION
The AI system shall verify catastrophic forgetting mitigation by test.
The test shall demonstrate that the implemented mitigations (such as elastic
weight consolidation, progressive neural networks, or replay buffers appropriate to
the model architecture and learning paradigm) retain previously-validated
capabilities after continuous learning episodes.
Success Criteria: The verification shall be considered successful when the test
shows that catastrophic forgetting mitigations retain previously-validated
capabilities after continuous learning episodes.

entries.title: Learning Validation
entries.text:
[R.AI-13.5] LEARNING VALIDATION
The AI system shall validate continuous learning updates against benchmark
performance criteria before the updated model becomes the operational model.
Updates that fail validation shall be rejected and the prior validated model retained.
Rationale: Without pre-activation validation, learning updates that produce
degraded behavior become operational before the degradation is detected. Pre-activation validation is the gate that prevents this.
[V.AI-13.5] LEARNING VALIDATION
The AI system shall verify learning validation by test.
The test shall demonstrate that continuous learning updates are validated against
benchmark performance criteria before becoming the operational model, that
updates failing validation are rejected with the prior validated model retained, and
that accepted updates meet or exceed prior performance on the benchmark suite.
Success Criteria: The verification shall be considered successful when the test
shows that learning validation rejects updates that fail benchmark criteria, and
accepted updates meet or exceed prior performance on the benchmark suite.

entries.title: Rollback Procedures
entries.text:
[R.AI-13.6] ROLLBACK PROCEDURES
The AI system shall implement rollback procedures that restore a prior validated
model state when continuous learning updates produce degraded performance
after activation. Rollback shall be invokable both automatically (on threshold-triggered detection) and manually (by qualified operator authority).
Rationale: Pre-activation validation reduces but does not eliminate the risk of
degraded learning outcomes reaching operations. Rollback procedures provide the
recovery path when post-activation degradation is detected.
[V.AI-13.6] ROLLBACK PROCEDURES
The AI system shall verify rollback procedures by test.
The test shall demonstrate that rollback restores a prior validated model state
when continuous learning updates produce degraded performance after activation,
invokable both automatically (on threshold-triggered detection) and manually (by
qualified operator authority).
Success Criteria: The verification shall be considered successful when the test
shows that rollback restores the prior validated model state both automatically
under threshold scenarios and on manual operator command.

entries.title: Odd Evolvability Declaration
entries.text:
[R.AI-13.7] ODD EVOLVABILITY DECLARATION
The AI system shall declare its ODD evolvability per AI-1.0, specifying whether the
operational design domain is permitted to evolve through continuous learning, the
bounds within which evolution may occur, and the conditions that trigger ODD
reassessment.
Rationale: Continuous learning that changes the model’s effective operational
envelope changes the system’s ODD. Without explicit ODD evolvability declaration,
the relationship between continuous learning and the validated operational
envelope is implicit and unverifiable.
[V.AI-13.7] ODD EVOLVABILITY DECLARATION
The AI system shall verify the ODD evolvability declaration by inspection.
The inspection shall confirm the declaration specifies, per AI-1.0, whether the
operational design domain is permitted to evolve through continuous learning, the
bounds within which evolution may occur, and the conditions that trigger ODD
reassessment, and that the declaration is consistent with the AI-1.0 ODD
declaration.
Success Criteria: The verification shall be considered successful when the
inspection shows that ODD evolvability is declared and consistent with the AI-1.0
ODD declaration, and the bounds and trigger conditions are documented.

entries.title: Continuous Learning Audit Trail
entries.text:
[R.AI-13.8] CONTINUOUS LEARNING AUDIT TRAIL
The AI system shall maintain an audit trail of all continuous learning events,
including data sources used for each learning event, parameter updates applied,
validation outcomes, and any rollback actions taken.
Rationale: Post-incident analysis, certification surveillance, and operational
accountability require complete reconstruction of the system’s learning history.
[V.AI-13.8] CONTINUOUS LEARNING AUDIT TRAIL
The AI system shall verify the continuous learning audit trail by inspection.
The inspection shall confirm the audit trail records the data sources used for each
learning event, the parameter updates applied, the validation outcomes, and any
rollback actions taken, and that records are retained per AI-1.8 (Classification
Compliance Audit Trail).
Success Criteria: The verification shall be considered successful when the
inspection shows that the continuous learning audit trail is complete, accurate, and
retained per AI-1.8 (Classification Compliance Audit Trail).

entries.title: Privacy implementation guidance
entries.text:
5.4 PRIVACY AND DATA PROTECTION IMPLEMENTATION GUIDANCE
This section provides implementation guidance for the privacy and data protection
requirements established under AI-10. AI systems often process personal data at
scale and may infer attributes operators did not explicitly intend to expose.
Implementation should anticipate both the data the system processes directly and
the inferences it can derive.

entries.title: Privacy implementation guidance: Data Minimization
entries.text:
5.4.1 Data Minimization
Implementation of [R.AI-10] data minimization principles should begin at the data
ingestion boundary. Where the operational task can be accomplished without
personal data, personal data should not enter the AI processing path. Where
personal data is required, the minimum sufficient subset should be retained and the
remainder discarded or replaced with derived features. Data minimization should
be a design-time decision, not a post-hoc filter.

entries.title: Privacy implementation guidance: Deidentification and Re-Identification Risk
entries.text:
5.4.2 De-identification and Re-Identification Risk
De-identification techniques (k-anonymity, l-diversity, differential privacy, synthetic
data generation) should be selected based on the threat model and the system’s
classification tier. Safety-Critical AI processing personal data should assume re-identification attempts will occur and select techniques whose privacy guarantees
survive the assumed adversary capabilities. Re-identification risk should be re-
evaluated whenever the input data distribution or the auxiliary data available to
potential adversaries materially changes.

entries.title: Privacy implementation guidance: Access Controls and Audit
entries.text:
5.4.3 Access Controls and Audit
Access to personal data within the AI processing path should be controlled, logged,
and auditable. Access logs should be retained per the AI-1.8 Classification
Compliance Audit Trail and should include both human access (developers,
operators, auditors) and automated access (training pipelines, model serving
infrastructure, monitoring systems). Anomalous access patterns should trigger
investigation.

entries.title: Privacy implementation guidance: Data Retention
entries.text:
5.4.4 Data Retention
Personal data retention should be limited to the minimum period required for the
operational task and any legally mandated retention. Retention schedules should be
documented per data category and enforced through automated deletion where
possible. Aggregated or de-identified outputs derived from personal data may have
different retention requirements than the source data; both schedules should be
explicit.

entries.title: Privacy implementation guidance: Inference and Membership Concerns
entries.text:
5.4.5 Inference and Membership Concerns
AI systems can leak training data through inversion attacks, membership inference
attacks, and confidence-based extraction techniques. Implementation should
consider: differential privacy or related techniques during training where the threat
model warrants, output filtering or noise injection at inference time for sensitive
applications, and adversarial testing for membership inference vulnerabilities for
systems trained on sensitive data. The risk surface depends on model architecture,
training data sensitivity, and adversary access; all three should inform the
mitigation strategy.

entries.title: Privacy implementation guidance: Cross-Border Data Transfer
entries.text:
5.4.6 Cross-Border Data Transfer
Where personal data crosses jurisdictional boundaries, applicable data protection
regulations (GDPR, regional equivalents) apply in addition to the AI-10 requirements.
Implementation should document the legal basis for transfer, the safeguards
applied, and the data subject rights preserved. Cross-border considerations should
be addressed at design time, not as a post-hoc compliance overlay.

entries.title: Standards profile: ISO/IEC 5338:2023, AI system lifecycle processes
entries.text: ISO/IEC 5338:2023, AI system lifecycle processes, is the international standard that extends established system and software lifecycle process models to systems containing AI components, defining the processes that carry an AI system from concept through development, operation, maintenance, and retirement. The AI Requirements Framework lists ISO/IEC 5338:2023 as a normative reference in Table 1-9 to the stated extent of its invocation and no further: the terminology imported in Appendix A at the clauses cited there. The Appendix A glossary is aligned with ISO/IEC 5338:2023 and ISO/IEC 22989:2022 where applicable (Section 1.4): the framework's definitions of data drift, concept drift, and continuous validation are drawn from clause 6.4.14, and its security vocabulary (adversarial attack, data poisoning, input manipulation, model inversion, model theft) from clause 6.4.3. In the requirement areas, ISO/IEC 5338 appears in the General row of the Related Domain Standards blocks: AI-1 Operational and Data Foundations and AI-3 ML Test Coverage cite clause 6.4, AI-4 Continuous Validation and AI-6 Out-of-Distribution Detection cite clause 6.4.14, AI-7 Adversarial Robustness cites clause 6.4.3, and AI-11 Multi-Model Systems, AI-12 Neural Networks, and AI-13 Continuous Learning and Adaptation cite the standard generally. The framework supplements this lifecycle standard rather than replacing it: SCL requirements attach failure-mode-driven controls to the AI lifecycle that ISO/IEC 5338 defines.

entries.title: Standards profile: ISO/IEC 22989:2022, AI concepts and terminology
entries.text: ISO/IEC 22989:2022, artificial intelligence concepts and terminology, is the international standard that establishes the shared vocabulary for AI systems: what counts as an AI system, machine learning, training, and the related lifecycle and trustworthiness concepts. It is the terminology anchor of the AI Requirements Framework, listed as a normative reference in Table 1-9 to the stated extent of its invocation and no further: the terminology imported in Appendix A at the clauses cited there, and the machine learning definition at 3.3.5 invoked by the deletion test in Section 1.2.1 and Appendix B.1. The Appendix A glossary is aligned with ISO/IEC 22989:2022 per Section 1.4 and imports its definitions at clause level, including AI system (3.1.4, adapted), machine learning (3.3.5), continuous learning (3.1.9), the data terms (training, validation, test, and production data, 3.2.x), bias (3.5.4), and the trustworthiness properties controllability (3.5.6), explainability (3.5.7), predictability (3.5.8), and robustness (3.5.12). The applicability determination in Section 1.2 rests on the 3.3.5 definition of machine learning, and AI-13 Continuous Learning is a synthesis built in part on the 5.11.9.2 continuous learning provisions (Section 1.3.2). Requirement areas cite it in their General rows: AI-1 (clause 5), AI-2 (3.5.4), AI-4 (5.11.9), AI-5 (5.11), AI-8 (3.5.7), AI-9 (3.5.6 and 5.13 automation levels), AI-13 (5.11.9.2), and AI-11 and AI-12 generally. Where SCL tailors a definition, the glossary marks the entry as adapted or tailored and names the source clause.

entries.title: Standards profile: DO-178C, airborne software assurance
entries.text: RTCA DO-178C, Software Considerations in Airborne Systems and Equipment Certification, is the software assurance standard used in civil aviation: it defines lifecycle objectives whose rigor scales with the Design Assurance Level (DAL) assigned to the software. The AI Requirements Framework lists DO-178C as an informative reference in Table 1-10 with stated relevance of aviation software, so it carries no conformity burden under Section 1.3, and the framework positions itself as a supplement to it, not a replacement: DO-178C consumes system safety outputs to set software criticality, and SCL's AI requirements attach the AI-specific controls that its code-centric objectives do not reach. The framework draws on DO-178C in two structural places: the consequence-based classification tiers of Section 1.2.2 are a synthesis that draws on the DO-178C DAL scheme alongside NPR 8000.4C and ISO 26262 ASIL (Section 1.3.2), and the verification independence scaling of Section 4.5 follows the pattern DO-178C established. In the Aviation rows of the Related Domain Standards blocks, AI-1 Operational and Data Foundations cites DO-178C section 5 (software development), AI-3 ML Test Coverage cites section 6 (verification process), AI-4.7 Deployment Format Validation cites 6.4 and 11.5, AI-7.4 Model Integrity cites 11.5, and AI-12 Neural Networks cites 5.2 (software design process).

entries.title: Standards profile: ISO 26262, road vehicle functional safety
entries.text: ISO 26262 is the functional safety standard for road vehicles: it defines the automotive safety lifecycle and the ASIL scheme (Automotive Safety Integrity Level) that grades hazards and scales the rigor of the required development activities. The AI Requirements Framework lists ISO 26262 as an informative reference in Table 1-10 with stated relevance of automotive safety, so it carries no conformity burden under Section 1.3, and the framework supplements it rather than replacing it: ISO 26262-6 consumes system safety outputs to set software criticality, and SCL's requirements add the AI-specific controls. The framework draws on ISO 26262 structurally in the Section 1.2.2 classification tiers, a synthesis that draws on ASIL alongside DO-178C DAL and NPR 8000.4C consequence classification (Section 1.3.2), and AI-1.0 lists ISO 26262 ASIL as an example governing regulatory framework in the ODD's Regulatory and Operational Authorization attribute. In the Automotive rows of the Related Domain Standards blocks, AI-1 cites ISO 26262-6:2018 section 5 (software development), AI-1.9 AI Hazard Analysis Integration cites ISO 26262-3:2018 Clause 6 (hazard analysis and risk assessment), AI-3 cites 26262-6 section 9 (software unit verification), AI-4.7 cites 26262-6 section 11 (testing of the embedded software), and AI-11 and AI-12 cite 26262-6 section 7 (software architectural design).

entries.title: Standards profile: NIST AI RMF 1.0, AI risk management framework
entries.text: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1) is a voluntary US framework for managing risks from AI systems. It organizes AI risk management into four functions, GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE, each broken into numbered categories and subcategories, giving organizations a common risk taxonomy rather than a certifiable requirement set. The AI Requirements Framework lists NIST AI RMF 1.0 as an informative reference in Table 1-10 with stated relevance of risk taxonomy, which carries no conformity burden under Section 1.3, and cites it by function and category in the Cross-Domain row of nearly every requirement area per the Section 1.3.1 citation convention: AI-1 maps to MAP-1 through MAP-5, AI-2 to MANAGE-2.3, AI-3 to MEASURE-2, AI-4 to MEASURE-3 and MEASURE-4, AI-5 to MEASURE-2.7, AI-6 to MEASURE-2.6, AI-7 to MANAGE-2.2, AI-8 to MANAGE-4.3, and AI-9 to GOVERN-1.5 and MANAGE-2.1, with further subcategory citations at the sub-requirement level. These citations support crosswalks for organizations already using the RMF; SCL certification itself is conducted against the framework's own requirements. The RMF's Generative AI Profile, NIST AI 600-1, is a Table 1-10 reference document and supplies the framework's definition of hallucination used in AI-5 (confabulation, section 2.2).

entries.title: Standards profile: ISO 21448, safety of the intended functionality (SOTIF)
entries.text: ISO 21448:2022, safety of the intended functionality (SOTIF), is the road-vehicle standard that addresses hazards arising not from component faults but from functional insufficiencies and performance limitations of the intended function, the failure territory where machine-learning-based functions typically live. In the AI Requirements Framework, ISO 21448 is cited as an informative domain standard in the Automotive rows of the Related Domain Standards blocks, per the Section 1.3.1 convention under which inline domain citations support cross-regulatory recognition while the Table 1-9 references remain the normative basis. Nine entries cite it: AI-1 Operational and Data Foundations (section 6), AI-1.9 AI Hazard Analysis Integration (the standard as a whole), AI-3 ML Test Coverage (section 7, evaluation), AI-4 Continuous Validation (section 13, field monitoring), AI-4.7 Deployment Format Validation (section 12), AI-5 Hallucination Prevention (section 7, functional insufficiencies and triggering conditions), AI-6 Out-of-Distribution Detection (sections 6 through 8), AI-11 Multi-Model Systems (section 5), and AI-13 Continuous Learning (section 13, operation phase activities). SOTIF also belongs to the ODD lineage: it took up the operational scoping concept that SAE J3016 introduced for driving automation, the same concept AI-1.0 generalizes into a domain-agnostic ODD declaration.

entries.title: Standards profile: NPR 7150.2D, NASA software engineering requirements
entries.text: NPR 7150.2D, NASA Software Engineering Requirements, is NASA's agency-level procedural requirements document for software: it governs software engineering across the full lifecycle, with requirements scaled by NASA's software classification scheme. The AI Requirements Framework, anchored in human-spaceflight-grade practice, lists NPR 7150.2D as a reference document in Table 1-10 with stated relevance of software lifecycle reference, and supplements it rather than replacing it. Two structural uses stand out. First, the Section 1.3.2 extension example: the Operations row of Table 1-7 extends NPR 7150.2D section 4 (software lifecycle, including operations, maintenance, and retirement) to host the framework's AI-specific continuous activities, AI-2.4 bias monitoring, the AI-4 family of continuous validation, AI-6.2 runtime out-of-distribution detection, and AI-9.6 operator role verification. Second, Section 1.2 notes that the software-item granularity used for the framework's determination boundary is established practice under NPR 7150.2. In the Aerospace rows, AI-4.7, AI-11, AI-12, and AI-13 cite NPR 7150.2D section 4, each noting where NASA's requirements do not address the AI-specific case (multi-model architecture, neural networks, continuous learning) and the framework is therefore framework-defined.

entries.title: Standards profile: SAE J3016, driving automation taxonomy and ODD origin
entries.text: SAE J3016 is the taxonomy standard for driving automation on public roads: it defines the six levels of driving automation, Level 0 through Level 5, and the supporting vocabulary of the automated-vehicle field. Its most exported concept is the Operational Design Domain (ODD), the declared conditions under which an automated system is designed to operate. The ODD lineage runs through J3016: it defined ODD for driving automation (clause 3.16), later automated-vehicle safety work including ISO 21448 (SOTIF) and the ODD attribute taxonomy of ISO 34503 took the concept up, and analogous operational-envelope thinking appears in aviation guidance. The AI Requirements Framework adapts the concept rather than adopting it: per Section 1.3.2, the ODD of AI-1.0 is adapted from SAE J3016 clause 3.16 and modified into a domain-agnostic AI ODD declaration, adding the Operational Claim summary, the eight attribute categories of Table 2.1.0-A, the five exclusion sub-categories of Table 2.1.0-B, and the framework-defined Subject Population and User Population distinction. The Appendix A glossary aligns its ODD definition with J3016 and ISO 34503. J3016 is also cited in the Automotive rows of AI-8.3 (clause 5.3), AI-9 (clause 5, automation levels), AI-9.1 (clause 5.2, dynamic driving task fallback), AI-9.7 (clause 8), AI-9.8 (clause 5.3), and AI-9.9 (clause 8.3, user training).

entries.title: SCL note: nondeterministic AI inside a declared boundary
entries.text: SCL published note, explanatory and not normative framework text. Certifying a nondeterministic system does not mean grading it against a single correct output for every input. The framework accepts that AI outputs may be nondeterministic and that identical inputs may not produce identical outputs (Section 1.2.1, Table 1-2); what it requires is a verification approach designed for that behavior. The certification claim is bounded first by the Operational Design Domain (AI-1.0), declared up front with an Operational Claim, which scopes the claim to declared conditions so that the certificate never appears to attest to behavior under all conditions. Inside that envelope the framework does not demand determinism. It demands evidence that behavior stays within defined bounds: testing across representative operational input distributions derived from the ODD (AI-3.3), run as tests whose quantitative measurements are evaluated against pass/fail criteria (Section 4.1); project-defined thresholds for minimum performance, confidence, data drift, out-of-distribution detection, and human escalation, each derived from and bounded by the ODD (Section 1.5); calibrated confidence indication for outputs that are nondeterministic or carry uncertainty, which the applicability table names as the verification emphasis (AI-8.3); output validity boundaries that catch operationally invalid outputs regardless of cause (AI-4.4); and hallucination detection and response (AI-5, AI-5.3). Because validated performance may not persist, the bounds are monitored in operation: data drift monitoring (AI-4.1), performance threshold maintenance (AI-4.2), out-of-distribution detection with human review or defined fallback (AI-6, AI-6.3), and proxy validation where ground truth is unavailable (AI-4.6). The requirement is bounded and monitored behavior, not eliminated variance. The outcome of an assessment is a formal determination against the applicable requirements at the time of assessment, Certified or Not Certified, and it is not a numerical grade. SCL separately reports the quantified risk measure defined in Appendix D, which reflects assessed residual risk and does not determine the certification outcome.

entries.title: SCL note: what an evaluation harness or benchmark does not cover
entries.text: SCL published note, explanatory and not normative framework text. An evaluation harness or benchmark measures how a model performs on a fixed set of tasks at a moment in time. That is useful for comparing tools and catching regressions, and the framework's own Test method works the same way: execution of the system under controlled conditions with defined inputs, producing quantitative measurements evaluated against pass/fail criteria (Section 4.1). Certification is a different object. Each requirement carries a co-located verification statement that names the method, the success criteria, and the evidence artifact it produces, implemented through the Verification Matrix and the Appendix C templates for the test report with its pass/fail determination, the inspection record, the applicability determination record, and the ODD declaration record (Section 4.0, Appendix C). Certification then adds what a harness run does not cover: a declared Operational Design Domain that bounds the claim (AI-1.0), continuous and periodic verification through the Operations and Sustainment phase (Section 4.4), data drift monitoring (AI-4.1) and performance threshold maintenance (AI-4.2) against validated baselines, hallucination response that keeps flagged outputs from being acted on without human review or defined fallback (AI-5.3), and operational role verification that checks whether operators still use the outputs as classified (AI-9.6). Harness or benchmark results can serve as test evidence inside a certification, recorded on the test report template, but a benchmark result is not a certification, because it carries no determination against the applicable requirements at the time of assessment, and a certification determination is a finding against requirements, not a leaderboard number. For language model systems with a retrieval pipeline, the framework treats the retrieval corpus as behavior-determining content subject to provenance, screening, and change control (AI-1.10), and it names retrieval-augmented generation pipelines among its examples of multi-model systems, with the AI-11 sub-requirements applying where two or more interacting AI models are present (AI-11).

entries.title: SCL note: applicability is a test, not a definition
entries.text: SCL published note, explanatory and not normative framework text. Whether a system needs certification is not answered by a terminology standard. ISO/IEC 22989:2022 is the terminology anchor of the framework: it supplies the vocabulary, the Appendix A glossary imports its definitions at clause level, and the applicability determination rests on its definition of machine learning (Section 1.3, Section 1.4). A definition, though, describes what a system is made of. Applicability is a question about what the system does, and the framework answers it with a test run against the system rather than a label. The test is the AI presence gate of Section 1.2.1 (Table 1-2), with its checklist form in Appendix B. The anchor criterion is learned behavior: system behavior specified by an artifact induced from data, through training, fine-tuning, continuous learning, or retrieval augmentation for example, rather than by an explicitly written specification against which correctness can be fully verified by established methods. The determination is made by inspection of how correctness can be established, on a declared determination boundary, with the evidence inspected cited in the Applicability Determination Record (Appendix C.1). Nondeterministic outputs and potential drift are supporting indicators only; they sharpen verification emphasis but do not establish applicability on their own, so a Kalman filter stays outside the framework when its dynamics, noise models, and covariances are explicitly specified (Table 1-2b). If correctness can be fully verified against an explicit specification by established methods, with no residual reliance on fidelity to a learned artifact, the system is not AI for the framework's purposes and standard software assurance applies. If the anchor criterion is met, classification follows in Section 1.2.2 and turns on decision consequence, whether outputs affect human safety, operational success, or neither, which selects the applicable requirement areas (Appendix B). The governing regulatory regime, such as an EU AI Act risk class, is recorded in the Operational Design Domain declaration (AI-1.0), separately from the presence determination.

entries.title: SCL note: where the developer's intent goes in an AI system
entries.text: SCL published note, explanatory and not normative framework text. Every system starts with intent. In traditional software the intent goes into the code: a developer who decides that a word means spam writes a rule that says so, and a reviewer can read the rule and trace it to a requirement. In an AI system the intent goes into the loss function instead. The developer labels the examples and defines a single number that says how wrong the last guess was, and training adjusts the parameters until that number gets smaller. It is the game of warmer or colder played by a machine: nobody says turn left, and the route the system finds is its own. What comes out is a set of weights, coordinates in a space the developer never drew. The word the developer had in mind dissolves into those coordinates, so you cannot grep for intent. The artifact holds the same knowledge the rule would have, in a form that cannot be read back. The framework states the consequence directly: traditional software has direct traceability from requirements to code, and AI systems break that traceability because behavior emerges from training data (AI-1); there is no code to cover in a neural network's weights (AI-3); and decisions come from learned patterns in weights that are not directly interpretable (AI-8). Traditional assurance assumes deterministic, logic-based systems with stable behavior after deployment, and AI challenges that through probabilistic outputs, which some vocabularies call nondeterministic, emergent behavior from training data, and potential performance degradation over time, so the framework defines requirements for the failure modes traditional verification does not cover (Section 1.1). Whether a system has crossed this line is a behavioral test of whether its behavior is learned from data rather than explicitly specified (Table 1-2, note-applicability-test). What to verify once the artifact cannot be read is the subject of note-verify-the-envelope.

entries.title: SCL note: if you cannot read the model, verify the envelope
entries.text: SCL published note, explanatory and not normative framework text. Traditional verification depends on a chain that is readable at every link: intent becomes requirements, requirements become code, code runs against tests, and each step traces to the last. AI breaks that chain in the middle. The intent went into the loss function and came out as weights that cannot be read (note-where-intent-goes), so correctness cannot be established by code inspection alone (Section 1.2.1, Table 1-2). If you cannot read the artifact, you verify the envelope around it, and the framework is that idea turned into requirements. First, the conditions the model was trained under: documented data provenance (AI-1.3), a characterized training distribution as the baseline for operational inputs (AI-6.1), and testing across representative operational input distributions (AI-3.3). Second, the conditions it operates under: an Operational Design Domain declared up front with an Operational Claim, which scopes the certification claim to declared conditions (AI-1.0); data drift monitored against the training baseline (AI-4.1); performance held above defined thresholds in operation (AI-4.2); and out-of-distribution detection (AI-6) with human review or defined fallback before autonomous action (AI-6.3). Third, the mechanisms that catch it when it fails: hallucination response that keeps flagged outputs from being acted on without human review or fallback (AI-5.3), output validity boundaries that catch operationally invalid outputs regardless of cause (AI-4.4), and human oversight with final decision authority, including periodic verification that operators still use outputs as classified (AI-9, AI-9.6). The artifact stays opaque and probabilistic, nondeterministic in the alias vocabulary. The envelope does not. A certificate records that the applicable requirements were met at the time of assessment; it does not claim the system is safe or that the weights are correct.
keywords: intent to requirements to code to tests

entries.title: SCL note: how an improving system still fails
entries.text: SCL published note, explanatory and not normative framework text. A spam filter is retrained weekly on incoming mail and learns that new terms correlate with spam. Detection goes up. Then the finance team sends legitimate mail about a crypto policy update, the model learns that pattern too, and it starts blocking internal finance communications. The loss function improved, detection is up, and the system is blocking legitimate business. The natural response is to record every update, compare versions, require sign off before release, and run regression tests after each cycle. That is correct but not sufficient: the things compared are two sets of weights, neither readable, and a regression test of aggregate accuracy reports that accuracy went up while the model learned to block your own finance team. The framework adds monitoring aimed at behavior: drift measured against baseline training distributions and alerted at defined thresholds (AI-4.1); performance held above thresholds derived from mission risk tolerance, with degradation triggering a defined mitigation response (AI-4.2); documented retraining and update trigger criteria with version control, regression testing requirements and change history (AI-4.3); and verification continuing through Operations and Sustainment (Section 4.4). Usage drifts too, when operators treat advisory outputs as authoritative, so operational role is periodically verified (AI-9.6). After certification, SCL surveillance checks that this monitoring is working; the FAQ entry "What happens after we are certified?" gives the cadence and reassessment triggers, including a drift threshold breach. Where learning continues in the field, AI-13.1 requires declared permission criteria and tier-scaled controls. A determination document is issued regardless of outcome and records the formal determination, Certified or Not Certified, at the time of assessment; a certificate does not claim the system is safe or that it will not fail.
keywords: worse for the people using it

entries.title: The EU AI Act: what it is and when its rules apply
entries.text:
SCL explainer, plain-language background and not legal advice, as of 2 October 2026. Prepared with AI assistance and reviewed by SCL.
The EU AI Act, officially Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, is a binding European Union law on artificial intelligence that applies directly in every EU country. Its rules depend on risk: it bans some AI uses and sets strict duties for high-risk AI (not yet in force). The European Commission says the Act sets no rules for minimal-risk AI, most AI in the EU.
The European Parliament and the Council of the EU passed it on a Commission proposal. The Commission's AI Office enforces the rules for general-purpose AI models (models that can do many kinds of tasks), and each EU country's authorities handle most other AI systems.
The Act entered into force on 1 August 2024. Its first bans have applied since 2 February 2025, and rules for general-purpose AI models since 2 August 2025. An amendment in force since 27 July 2026 delayed the main high-risk rules to 2 December 2027 or 2 August 2028, depending on the system. Most other rules have applied since 2 August 2026, when chatbots had to start saying they are AI. It also added a ban, from 2 December 2026, on AI that makes non-consensual sexual content or child sexual abuse material. As of 2 October 2026, the high-risk rules and that new ban have not started.
The Act reaches beyond the EU, covering developers anywhere that offer AI in the EU and some non-EU AI whose output is used there.
Official sources: the law, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32024R1689, its amendment, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32026R1744, and the Commission's page, https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai.
Sources: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32024R1689, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32026R1744, https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai, https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/enforcement-ai-act, https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/ai-omnibus-enters-force, https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/commission-starts-enforcing-ai-act-rules-and-new-transparency-requirements-2-august

entries.title: How to read a Federal Register document
entries.text:
SCL explainer, plain-language background and not legal advice, as of 2 October 2026. Prepared with AI assistance and reviewed by SCL.
The Federal Register is the US government's daily journal of agency rules, proposed rules, notices and presidential documents. As of 2 October 2026, the National Archives' Office of the Federal Register publishes it every federal business day. The issuing agency (or the President) decides what each document says; the Office publishes it but cannot interpret it.
Every document falls into one of four categories. A rule (also called a regulation) has legal effect. A proposed rule invites comment but has no legal effect; only the final rule, which can differ, binds. A notice shares information, such as a meeting, and imposes no general legal requirements. Presidential documents, such as executive orders, come from the President; later orders can amend or revoke earlier ones.
In a rule or proposed rule, the ACTION heading names the document type. SUMMARY is a short plain overview, not the rule itself. DATES gives the comment deadline or the effective date (when a rule takes effect, usually after publication). Comment periods usually run 30, 60 or 90 days, and comments go to the issuing agency.
A document number, such as 2026-20281, identifies one published document. A docket number is the agency's own file number, usually shared by the proposed and final rule.
Agency policy statements and interpretations of the law, often called guidance, lack the force of law, even when printed in the Rules section.
FederalRegister.gov is an unofficial copy; the official edition is in print and on govinfo.gov. Official sources: archives.gov and govinfo.gov.
Sources: https://www.archives.gov/federal-register/the-federal-register/about.html, https://www.federalregister.gov/reader-aids/government-policy-and-ofr-procedures/about-this-site#legal-status, https://www.archives.gov/federal-register/faqs, https://www.archives.gov/files/federal-register/write/handbook/ddh.pdf, https://www.govinfo.gov/help/fr, https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2019/08/08/2019-16946/adoption-of-recommendations

entries.title: What "high risk" means for AI
entries.text:
SCL explainer, plain-language background and not legal advice, as of 2 October 2026. Prepared with AI assistance and reviewed by SCL.
"High risk" is not a general rating of AI. It is one of four risk levels in the European Union's AI Act, from banned to minimal or no risk. The European Commission says most AI in the EU, such as spam filters, is minimal or no risk.
AI becomes high risk in two ways. It may be a product, or a safety part of one, that must pass an independent check under EU product-safety law, such as some medical devices. Or it may serve a use listed in the Act, such as hiring, education, credit scoring or border control. A listed system doing only a narrow procedural task is not high risk unless it profiles people.
EU lawmakers wrote the list; the European Commission can update it. The developer (called the provider) classifies its own system first; a national regulator can overrule it.
High risk does not mean banned, but such systems will face strict rules, including risk assessment, data quality, logging and human oversight. As of 2 October 2026, the main high-risk rules do not yet apply. A 2026 amendment delayed them to 2 December 2027 for listed uses and 2 August 2028 for AI in products.
Other frameworks differ. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) publishes a voluntary AI Risk Management Framework, not a law. Under it, each organisation decides which of its own AI risks are highest.
Official sources: the AI Act on EUR-Lex, the Commission's AI Act page, and NIST's framework page.
Sources: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/2026-07-27/eng, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj/eng, https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework, https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.100-1.pdf

entries.title: Regulations, standards, guidance and certificates: what is the difference?
entries.text:
SCL explainer, plain-language background and not legal advice, as of 2 October 2026. Prepared with AI assistance and reviewed by SCL.
Regulations are legally binding; standards and guidance on their own are not. In the US, federal agencies write regulations, using powers Congress grants by law. Examples of guidance include FDA guidance documents, FAA advisory circulars and the European Commission's guidelines on banned AI practices. FDA says a company may take another approach that meets the law.
Standards bodies such as ISO, a non-governmental organization, write standards. A standard becomes legally required only when a law or regulation adopts it, and only where that law applies. In the US this is called incorporation by reference, and only the named edition becomes binding. For example, since 2 February 2026 FDA's medical device quality rule has required the makers it covers to document a quality management system meeting ISO 13485:2016.
In the EU, a high-risk AI system following a harmonised standard listed in the EU's Official Journal is presumed to meet the matching AI Act requirements, though makers may comply another way. As of 2 October 2026, those requirements do not yet apply; they start on 2 December 2027 or 2 August 2028, depending on the system.
A certificate is an independent body's written assurance that a particular product, service or system meets specific requirements. ISO certifies no one; outside certification bodies do. A certificate does not replace a regulator: an ISO 13485 certificate does not exempt a manufacturer from FDA inspection. Certificates can also expire or be withdrawn.
Official sources: the US Office of the Federal Register, FDA, ISO and EUR-Lex.
Sources: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-A/part-10/subpart-B/section-10.115, https://www.iso.org/sites/ConsumersStandards/1_standards.html, https://www.archives.gov/files/federal-register/write/handbook/ibr.pdf, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:02024R1689-20260727, https://www.iso.org/certification.html, https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/quality-management-system-regulation-qmsr/quality-management-system-regulation-frequently-asked-questions
keywords: which edition of a standard applies

entries.title: Is AI regulated in the US, and who makes the rules?
entries.text:
SCL explainer, plain-language background and not legal advice, as of 2 October 2026. Prepared with AI assistance and reviewed by SCL.
As of 2 October 2026, the US regulates AI in pieces, with no comprehensive federal AI law or AI regulator. Rules come from Congress, the President, agencies and the states.
Congress has targeted specific harms. The TAKE IT DOWN Act (2025) makes it a federal crime, in certain cases, to knowingly publish intimate images without consent, including AI-generated fakes. Since May 2026 the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has enforced the law's 48-hour takedown duty for platforms.
Presidents instruct agencies through executive orders. President Biden's 2023 AI order was revoked in January 2025. A December 2025 order calls for national AI rules made with Congress. Until then, it directs action against state AI laws the administration considers too burdensome, including Justice Department lawsuits. Congress has not overridden state AI laws. A June 2026 order directed agencies to design a voluntary scheme giving the government early access to certain advanced models.
Agencies apply existing powers. The FTC finalized $930,000 in settlements in August 2026 over allegedly false claims to offer an AI-powered service. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) checks AI-enabled medical devices through the FDA's device reviews. NIST, a federal standards agency, publishes a voluntary AI Risk Management Framework: guidance, not regulation.
States such as California and Texas write their own AI laws. In May 2026 Colorado replaced its 2024 AI Act with a law on automated tools used in decisions about jobs, lending, health care and more, with developer duties from 2027.
Official sources: federalregister.gov, govinfo.gov, whitehouse.gov, ftc.gov, fda.gov, leg.colorado.gov.
Sources: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/12/16/2025-23092/ensuring-a-national-policy-framework-for-artificial-intelligence, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-119publ12/html/PLAW-119publ12.htm, https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/03.20.26-National-Policy-Framework-for-Artificial-Intelligence-Legislative-Recommendations.pdf, https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/08/ftc-finalizes-orders-cox-media-group-two-other-firms-settling-charges-they-deceived-customers-about, https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/digital-health-center-excellence/artificial-intelligence-enabled-medical-devices, https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/sb26-189

entries.title: Who checks that AI products are safe?
entries.text:
SCL explainer, plain-language background and not legal advice, as of 2 October 2026. Prepared with AI assistance and reviewed by SCL.
Who checks an AI product depends on what it is. In the US, medical devices, vehicles and aircraft each have their own regulator, and each checks differently.
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regulates medical devices and lists the AI-enabled devices it has authorized. One route to market is the 510(k): the maker shows a device is substantially equivalent to one already legally sold, and FDA then clears it. Clearance is not FDA approval, a stricter route for the highest-risk devices.
Cars and trucks, including automated ones, use self-certification: each manufacturer certifies that its vehicles meet every applicable federal safety standard. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) does not approve or certify them.
For aircraft, a company seeking a type certificate for a design must show it meets the airworthiness (safe-to-fly) requirements of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), and the FAA must make its own finding. As of 2 October 2026, the FAA still points to the FAA's own July 2024 AI safety roadmap, a plan rather than a rule, which says to use existing aviation safety requirements.
Independent bodies can also certify that a product or system meets specific requirements. ISO, the International Organization for Standardization, writes standards but certifies no one, so no company can be certified by ISO. ISO advises checking whether a certifier is accredited, meaning its competence has been independently confirmed, though accreditation is not compulsory.
Official sources: FDA, NHTSA in the Federal Register, the Electronic Code of Federal Regulations, FAA and ISO.
Sources: https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/premarket-submissions-selecting-and-preparing-correct-submission/premarket-notification-510k, https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/artificial-intelligence-enabled-medical-devices/list-artificial-intelligence-enabled-medical-devices, https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/09/21/2026-19242/federal-motor-vehicle-safety-standards-denial-of-a-petition-for-rulemaking, https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-21/subpart-B/section-21.21, https://www.faa.gov/aircraft/air_cert/step/roadmap_for_AI_safety_assurance, https://www.iso.org/certification.html

entries.title: NPR 7150.2D 1.1 Overview (part 1 of 2)
entries.text:
Verbatim excerpt from NPR 7150.2D, NASA Software Engineering Requirements, published by NASA, Office of the Chief Engineer, effective 2022-03-08 (expires 2027-03-08): Chapter 1: Introduction, section 1.1 Overview, part 1 of 2. NASA's text, not SCL framework text and not an SCL requirement; square-bracket tags are shown in parentheses. Source: https://nodis3.gsfc.nasa.gov/displayDir.cfm?t=NPR&c=7150&s=2D

1.1.1 This directive imposes requirements on procedures, design considerations, activities, and tasks used to acquire, develop, maintain, operate, retire, and manage applicable software. This directive is a designed set of requirements for protecting the ’Agency’s investment in software engineering products and fulfilling our responsibility to the citizens of the United States (U.S.).
1.1.2 The requirements in this directive have been extracted from industry standards and proven NASA experience in software engineering. Centers and software developers may show that many of the requirements are satisfied through existing programs, procedures, and processes.
1.1.3 The Agency makes significant investments in software engineering to support the Agency’s investment areas: Space Flight, Aeronautics, Research and Technology, Information Technology (IT), and Institutional Infrastructure. NASA ensures that programs, projects, systems, and subsystems that use software follow a standard set of requirements. One of the goals of this directive is to bring the Agency’s engineering and software development and management communities together to optimize resources and talents across Center boundaries. For NASA to effectively communicate and work seamlessly across Centers, a common framework of generic requirements is needed. This directive fulfills this need for the Agency within the discipline of software engineering.
1.1.4 This directive does not require a specific software life cycle model. Where this NPR refers to phases and milestone reviews in the software life cycle, it uses the standard NASA life cycle models described in NPR 7120.5, NASA Space Flight Program and Project Management Requirements, NPR 7120.7, NASA Information Technology Program and Project Management Requirements, and NPR 7120.8, NASA Research and Technology Program and Project Management Requirements, as supported by milestone reviews described in NPR 7123.1, NASA Systems Engineering Processes and Requirements.

entries.title: NPR 7150.2D 1.1 Overview (part 2 of 2)
entries.text:
Verbatim excerpt from NPR 7150.2D, NASA Software Engineering Requirements, published by NASA, Office of the Chief Engineer, effective 2022-03-08 (expires 2027-03-08): Chapter 1: Introduction, section 1.1 Overview, part 2 of 2. NASA's text, not SCL framework text and not an SCL requirement; square-bracket tags are shown in parentheses. Source: https://nodis3.gsfc.nasa.gov/displayDir.cfm?t=NPR&c=7150&s=2D

1.1.5 NASA is committed to instituting and updating these requirements to meet the Agency’s current and future challenges in software engineering. Successful experiences are codified in updated versions of this directive after experience has been gained through its use within the NASA software community, the collection of lessons learned from projects, and the implementation records of the Engineering Technical Authorities (ETAs).

entries.title: NPR 7150.2D 1.2 Hierarchy of NASA Software-Related Engineering and Program/Project Documents
entries.text:
Verbatim excerpt from NPR 7150.2D, NASA Software Engineering Requirements, published by NASA, Office of the Chief Engineer, effective 2022-03-08 (expires 2027-03-08): Chapter 1: Introduction, section 1.2 Hierarchy of NASA Software-Related Engineering and Program/Project Documents. NASA's text, not SCL framework text and not an SCL requirement; square-bracket tags are shown in parentheses. Source: https://nodis3.gsfc.nasa.gov/displayDir.cfm?t=NPR&c=7150&s=2D

1.2.1 Agency-Level Software Policies and Requirements
NPD 7120.4, NASA Engineering and Program/Project Management Policy, is an overarching directive that establishes top-level policies for all software created, acquired, or maintained by or for NASA, including Commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) software, Government-off-the-shelf (GOTS) software, and Modified-off-the-shelf (MOTS) software and open-source software, embedded software, reused software, legacy software, and heritage software. This directive supports the implementation of NPD 7120.4, and establishes the Agency set of software engineering requirements for software acquisition, development, maintenance, retirement, operations, and management. It provides a set of software engineering requirements in generic terms for use by NASA, contractors, grant recipients, or parties to agreements. Additional Agency-level project management requirements and systems engineering requirements exist that influence and affect the software development activities on a project. In the event of a conflict between an NPD and NPR, the NPD takes precedence.
1.2.2 Agency-Level Multi-Center and Product Line Requirements (non-software specific)
Existing Agency-Level NPDs and NPRs elaborate, tailor, and in some cases add requirements to those above to address the needs of major multi-Center projects, specific product lines, and specific focus areas. Examples of representative NPRs in this category are NPR 8705.2, Human-Rating Requirements for Space Systems, NPR 8715.3, NASA General Safety Program Requirements, NPR 8735.2, Hardware Quality Assurance Program Requirements for Programs and Projects, NPR 7120.5, NPR7123.1, NPD 2800.1, Managing Information Technology, NPR 2800.2, Information and Communication Technology Accessibility, and NPR 2810.1, Security of Information Technology.
1.2.3 Center-Level Directives or Requirements (related to software)
Center-level directives or requirements are developed by NASA Centers to document their local software policies, requirements, and procedures. These directives are responsive to the higher-level requirements while addressing the specific application areas and the Center’s mission within the Agency. In the event of a conflict between this NPR with a Center-level directive, the information provided in this NPR takes precedence.

entries.title: NPR 7150.2D 1.3 Document Structure (part 1 of 2)
entries.text:
Verbatim excerpt from NPR 7150.2D, NASA Software Engineering Requirements, published by NASA, Office of the Chief Engineer, effective 2022-03-08 (expires 2027-03-08): Chapter 1: Introduction, section 1.3 Document Structure, part 1 of 2. NASA's text, not SCL framework text and not an SCL requirement; square-bracket tags are shown in parentheses. Source: https://nodis3.gsfc.nasa.gov/displayDir.cfm?t=NPR&c=7150&s=2D

1.3.1 Chapter 2 describes the roles, responsibilities, and institutional requirements relevant to the requirements in this directive. This chapter describes the responsibilities for maintaining and advancing organizational capability in software engineering practices to effectively meet the scientific and technological objectives of the Agency. It defines the roles and responsibilities of key officials in software engineering management, the software development and management processes, and the software life cycle management processes. Specific software classification applicability, if any, for the requirements in Chapter 2 are contained in the requirement wording. The requirements in Chapter 2 are not part of the Requirements Mapping Matrix in Appendix C. Approval of any tailoring of requirements designated in Chapter 2 can be done by the appropriate organization per the defined roles and responsibilities.
1.3.2 Chapter 3 establishes software management requirements. The software management activities define and control the many software aspects of a project from beginning to end. The software management activities include the required interfaces to other organizations, determination of deliverables, cost estimates, tracking of schedules, risk management, formal and informal reviews, as well as other forms of verification and validation, and determination of the amount of supporting services. The planned management of these activities is captured in one or more software or system plans.
1.3.3 Chapter 4 provides the software engineering life cycle requirements. This directive makes no recommendation for a specific software life cycle model. Each has its strengths and weaknesses, and no one model is best for every situation. Whether using the agile methods, spiral model, the iterative model, waterfall, or any other development life cycle model, each has its own set of requirements, design, implementation, testing, release to operations, maintenance, and retirement. Although this directive does not impose a particular life cycle model on each software project, it does support a standard set of life cycle phases. Use of the different phases of a life cycle allows the various products of a project to be gradually developed and matured from initial concepts through the fielding of the product and to its final retirement.

entries.title: NPR 7150.2D 1.3 Document Structure (part 2 of 2)
entries.text:
Verbatim excerpt from NPR 7150.2D, NASA Software Engineering Requirements, published by NASA, Office of the Chief Engineer, effective 2022-03-08 (expires 2027-03-08): Chapter 1: Introduction, section 1.3 Document Structure, part 2 of 2.
